{"id": "24:37/q05", "question": "What is the relation between “trade” and “sale” here?", "turns_on": "Whether تجارة is a general category, buying, imported commerce, or an ongoing occupation determines how بيع relates to it.", "positions": [{"id": "24:37/q05/p1", "position": "Trade is buying and selling for profit, while sale is a named instance of it.", "reasons": "Kashshaf calls it the trader's craft; Bursevi cites al-Mufradat's capital-for-profit definition and its note that the Arabic word uniquely has tāʾ followed by jīm. Razi and Bursevi distinguish cash received in sale from goods acquired in purchase; Asad extends bayʿ to worldly gain."}, {"id": "24:37/q05/p2", "position": "Trade means buying; sale is the other half of commerce.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Waqidi and others infer the restriction from sale being named separately and cite 62:11. {"id": "24:37/q07", "question": "Why does trade receive special mention as a possible distraction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "24:37/q07/p1", "position": "It is the greatest or most widespread ordinary distraction from prayer and devotion.", "reasons": "Tha'labi's People of Meaning, Wahidi, Baghawi, Qurtubi and Bursevi make this point; Bursevi says no kind of trade can distract them."}, {"id": "24:37/q07/p2", "position": "The wording tests whether worldly gains and pleasures displace what lasts.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir says they prefer God's lasting reward to perishable possessions. {"id": "24:37/q08", "question": "What does trade's failure to distract them teach about their conduct?", "turns_on": "Whether the negation presupposes actual trade and how worldly activity relates to worship.", "positions": [{"id": "24:37/q08/p1", "position": "They may trade, but leave or subordinate it whenever remembrance, timely prayer and God's obligations call.", "reasons": "Yahya says they leave at the call. Abu al-Darda calls trading lawful."}, {"id": "24:37/q08/p2", "position": "They have no trade capable of distracting them.", "reasons": "Razi reports this; Nasafi likens them to a solitary devotee, Abu Hayyan to a beaconless road. {"id": "24:37/q09", "question": "What is “remembrance of God” here?", "turns_on": "Whether the following explicit mention of prayer repeats and specifies remembrance or shows remembrance has another sense.", "positions": [{"id": "24:37/q09/p1", "position": "The obligatory prayer, especially attending it when due.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Ibn Abbas, Ata, the two Muqatils, al-Suddi and others gloss it as the five prayers; Baghawi connects it to mosque attendance. Wahidi and Ibn Jawzi say the following clause then emphasizes keeping its time."}, {"id": "24:37/q09/p2", "position": "The call to prayer.", "reasons": "Yahya includes the call alongside five prayers; Mawardi attributes the narrower explanation to him, and Qurtubi reports it."}, {"id": "24:37/q09/p3", "position": "Spoken praise, supplication, God's names and oneness, with remembrance in heart and tongue.", "reasons": "Mawardi names the beautiful names; Ibn Jawzi reports remembrance on the tongue. {"id": "24:37/q10", "question": "Why is establishing prayer named after remembrance?", "turns_on": "Whether ذكر الله is identified with prayer or distinguished as inward or verbal remembrance.", "positions": [{"id": "24:37/q10/p1", "position": "If remembrance means prayer, the repetition stresses performing it at its appointed time and fulfilling its requirements.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Baghawi and Ibn Jawzi name timing; Biqai says even minimally adequate performance counts and the wording stresses the requirements, without demanding highest perfection."}, {"id": "24:37/q10/p2", "position": "Prayer is separate from remembrance, so naming both avoids redundancy.", "reasons": "Qurtubi argues explicitly for this; Tabataba'i calls remembrance inward knowledge opposite heedlessness and sees prayer as one outward duty."}, {"id": "24:37/q10/p3", "position": "Prayer and zakat show worship at fixed times alongside continuous remembrance.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i pairs sustained and single sales with continuous inward remembrance and time-bound acts."}]}
{"id": "24:37/q11", "question": "What does “establishing prayer” require, and which prayers does it include?", "turns_on": "The scope of إقامة ranges from due time and proper form to congregational performance or the religion as a whole; Razi distinguishes obligatory from voluntary prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "24:37/q11/p1", "position": "Performing prescribed prayer at its appointed time, without delay.", "reasons": "Ibrahim, Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Baghawi and others focus on timely attendance; Baghawi says delayed prayer is not properly established. Muqatil ibn Hayyan adds attending and guarding God's trust."}, {"id": "24:37/q11/p2", "position": "Completing prayer according to its due form and conditions.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi says complete it. Razi invokes all its due rights under 2:3; Ibn al-Shaykh requires pillars, conditions, sunnas and etiquettes, considering any omission a failure to establish. Ibn Jawzi joins completeness with due time."}, {"id": "24:37/q11/p3", "position": "The obligatory prayer in particular.", "reasons": "Abu al-Aliya names the obligation; Razi prefers obligatory prayer as the precise established legal term."}, {"id": "24:37/q11/p4", "position": "Both obligatory and voluntary prayer.", "reasons": "Razi reports Ibn Abbas's ḍuḥā example."}, {"id": "24:37/q11/p5", "position": "Prayer in congregation.", "reasons": "Al-Suddi says this directly; Ibn Kathir reports his congregational gloss of remembrance."}, {"id": "24:37/q11/p6", "position": "Establishing the religion.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Aslam gives this broader gloss."}]}

{"id": "25:2/q02", "question": "What does mulk over heaven and earth mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression is explained as sovereign power itself or through its technical distinction from ownership.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q02/p1", "position": "Sovereign rule and disposal over all heaven, earth, and their contents.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī specifies prevailing commands, judgments and rulings; Bursevī and al-Rāghib define mulk as command and prohibition among subjects. Al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı add creating, destroying, giving life and death. Al-Kāshifī grounds God's right to rule in His creation. Abū Ḥayyān links ownership in 24:64 to this added rule and subjection; Study Quran points to 67:1 and 36:83."}, {"id": "25:2/q02/p2", "position": "Mulk is rule over subjects, distinguished from the wider milk of ownership.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib says every mulk is milk, but not conversely; another distinction reserves milk for owning substance and mulk for other rule."}]}

{"id": "25:2/q04", "question": "What inward meaning is drawn from the kingdom?", "turns_on": "The two transmitted inward applications emphasize different paths to a share in kingship.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q04/p1", "position": "Obedience and preference for God give a person a share in the kingdom.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, as transmitted by al-Sulamī, connects devotion to participation in the kingdom."}, {"id": "25:2/q04/p2", "position": "Occupation with divine sovereignty makes one sovereign; occupation with kingship gains kingship and kingdom.", "reasons": "Al-Naṣrābādhī, as transmitted by al-Sulamī, distinguishes the fruits of these two orientations."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q05", "question": "Whose claim does 'He did not take a child' deny?", "turns_on": "The identified opponents and whether 'taking' points to adoption or all offspring differ.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q05/p1", "position": "It denies claims that Ezra, Jesus, or angels are God's children.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn ʿAbbās and others identify Jews' ʿUzayr, Christians' Messiah, and Arab pagans' angelic daughters; Ibn Abī Ḥātim's ʿIkrima also lists Sabeans worshipping angels, Magians worshipping sun and moon, and idolaters worshipping idols among those addressed. Al-Ṭabarī calls attribution of a child a lie. Study Quran cites 2:116 and 6:101–102."}, {"id": "25:2/q05/p2", "position": "It specifically answers Christian attribution of a son.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī singles out the Christians; al-Rāzī says an eternally worshipped God cannot have a successor."}, {"id": "25:2/q05/p3", "position": "It also rejects claims of divine offspring or adoption generally.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān names Quraysh, Christians, and Jews; Elmalılı explicitly includes biological offspring and adopted children. {"id": "25:2/q06", "question": "What does taking a child mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether ittakhadha highlights adoption or conveys the general impossibility of offspring.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q06/p1", "position": "It means adopting or assigning someone the status of a child.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explains the wording as assignment of child status; Abū Ḥayyān says God did not adopt anyone. Bursevī cites al-Mufradāt deriving ittakhadha from akhadha and notes walad can be singular or plural, young or old, male or female."}, {"id": "25:2/q06/p2", "position": "It denies having or begetting any child.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports an alternative like 'He did not beget,' because procreation is impossible for God; Elmalılı includes biological offspring as well as adopted children. {"id": "25:2/q07", "question": "Why can God have no child?", "turns_on": "The grounds offered are God's eternal sufficiency, nonbodily nature, and universal creation.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q07/p1", "position": "An eternal, all-powerful sovereign needs no child for help or inheritance.", "reasons": "Jishumī, al-Rāzī, Bursevī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reason that God does not die or need an heir; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds that a limited owner may need help in management, whereas God has total power. Islahi says He needs no helper. Al-Biqāʿī adds that no child could arrogantly resist His messenger."}, {"id": "25:2/q07/p2", "position": "God's nonbodily, intrinsic power rules out a child.", "reasons": "Jishumī says God is no body and is powerful, knowing and living in Himself, not by a distinct power; His ability to create heaven and earth excludes taking a child."}, {"id": "25:2/q07/p3", "position": "Because every other being is His creation and possession, none can be His child.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports Irshād al-ʿAql al-Salīm making universal creation the ground of both denials; al-Ṭībī compares 6:101."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q08", "question": "How is the child-denial joined and placed?", "turns_on": "The clause's coordination, position among four attributes, and antithesis each explain its form.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q08/p1", "position": "It is an independent denial, strategically placed between ownership and partner-denial.", "reasons": "Bursevī says it is coordinated with the preceding nominal clause. Al-Ālūsī says its placement establishes independent force rather than letting it seem merely a continuation of ownership. Elmalılı coordinates it with the partner-denial: adoption would lead to partnership. Ibn ʿĀshūr says four attributes frame two contested claims with two facts the audience accepted; he cites 23:86–87 and says wise action is never futile."}, {"id": "25:2/q08/p2", "position": "Its wording contrasts with the polytheists' taking other gods.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr describes a rhetorical antithesis between God's not taking a child and the polytheists taking deities in 25:3."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q09", "question": "Whose claims does the denial of a partner confront?", "turns_on": "The sources identify several historical opponents and specify the kind of rivalry or delegation rejected.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q09/p1", "position": "It rejects pagan partners, including angels or idols and the talbiya's subordinate partner.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies Arabs' angelic partners; al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim recount a pilgrimage formula allowing a partner owned by God. Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes this to Quraysh; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says pagans could acknowledge universal ownership yet imagine delegated, lesser lords. Al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī and Bursevī connect the denial to idolaters."}, {"id": "25:2/q09/p2", "position": "It expressly rejects dualist or Magian claims of multiple divine rulers.", "reasons": "Jishumī includes Christians, dualists and Magians in the paired denial. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı single out dualists; the last two say exclusive ownership already implies no partner but explicit denial answers two or three gods."}, {"id": "25:2/q09/p3", "position": "It excludes any rival or co-owner of sovereignty, whatever the claimant.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī denies a rival in greatness; Jishumī denies one able to thwart God's will. Al-Rāzī says this cuts off fear and hope directed to stars or idols. Bursevī cites a Mathnawī couplet mocking a claim of partnership; al-Qushayrī extends uniqueness to essence, works, reality and attributes."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q10", "question": "Why does God's kingdom admit no partner?", "turns_on": "The debate concerns whether sole ownership by itself rules out delegated lords, or whether universal creation supplies the decisive premise.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q10/p1", "position": "His unlimited, universal rule leaves no domain or need for a co-ruler.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says partnership would answer a limit in one's own rule, which God has none; Bursevī excludes a competitor or helper in creation. Elmalılı argues creatures cannot exceed their created bounds, whereas God's power is boundless; al-Biqāʿī says no partner could have a command or messenger outside God's realm."}, {"id": "25:2/q10/p2", "position": "Creation and determination entail direct governance, with no delegated divine affairs.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says bare ownership could coexist in pagan thought with delegated lords; because God creates and determines everything, He governs every affair. Prior and concurrent causes work within the order He determines."}, {"id": "25:2/q10/p3", "position": "Every alleged partner is itself created and owned by God.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says every object of worship is God's property; al-Ālūsī reports this as the explicit explanation of both denials, and al-Ṭībī invokes 6:101."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q11", "question": "What is meant by 'everything' that God created?", "turns_on": "Whether the universal requires a supplied restriction; both readings exclude God and eternal attributes.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q11/p1", "position": "All things capable of being described as created, including creatures and their actions.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, Jishumī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others qualify the universal by 'created'; al-Nasafī says the adjacent verb itself limits 'thing'. Abū Ḥayyān includes entities and acts and says ordinary universals need no explicit exception for the speaker: 'I honored every man' excludes the speaker. Ibn ʿĀshūr includes greatest and smallest existents; al-Biqāʿī includes alleged offspring and partners."}, {"id": "25:2/q11/p2", "position": "It requires an implicit qualification, 'everything whose creation is valid,' excluding God and eternal attributes.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports the proposal, then argues ordinary universal language already excludes the speaker, so no omitted words are needed."}]}

{"id": "25:2/q13", "question": "What does universal creation prove against rival creators?", "turns_on": "Whether the stress falls on excluding rival originators or on the governed limits of creatures.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q13/p1", "position": "God alone originates everything; light, darkness, Satan, and other beings are no second creator.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī names Magian and dualist light and darkness, Yazdān and Ahriman; al-Qurṭubī adds Satan and any creaturely power to originate. {"id": "25:2/q14", "question": "Does 'He created everything' include human acts?", "turns_on": "Whether acts fall under 'everything', how scriptural references to human creators are understood, and whether creation as apportionment can apply to acts.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q14/p1", "position": "Yes: acts are things, so their origination falls under God's creation and decree.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites 39:62 and 35:3 against countertexts naming servants creators and says the clause answers those who claim to create their own acts. {"id": "25:2/q15", "question": "Does universal creation include evil?", "turns_on": "Whether God's praise of creation excludes evil or concerns the display of power in creating it.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q15/p1", "position": "Yes; creating evil can display God's universal power even when evil itself is not praiseworthy.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī answers that origination from nonexistence and extinguishing beings manifest power. {"id": "25:2/q16", "question": "What does the verse imply about the Qur'an being created?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q16/p1", "position": "The Qur'an is created because it falls among created, measured things.", "reasons": "Jishumī states the inference; al-Nasafī adds that an agent possessing all its attributes cannot itself be an object acted upon, supporting both calling God a thing and calling the Qurʾān created."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q17", "question": "What does qaddara or taqdīr mean as a word?", "turns_on": "Whether taqdīr describes apportioning by an agent or a thing's settled measure.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q17/p1", "position": "To apportion, measure, determine, or ordain a thing.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī includes lifespans and provisions; Jishumī offers doing a thing according to measure. {"id": "25:2/q18", "question": "What did God determine for each created thing?", "turns_on": "The explanations emphasize fitted function, allotted term and decree, guidance, divine knowledge, cosmic constraints, or hidden stages; some overlap in individual sources.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q18/p1", "position": "Its fitting form, capacity, properties, and function, in wisdom and without defect.", "reasons": "Muqātil says each is made as it ought; al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq emphasize sustenance and establishment. Qatāda adds sound nature and benefit; al-Kalbī form and endpoint. Al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr stress precise preparation without flaw; humans are fitted for perception, religious and worldly duties, crafts and judgment. Asad compares 87:2–3; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 54:49 and 13:17. Abū Ḥayyān relays Ibn ʿAṭiyya's place, time, quantity, benefit and precision."}, {"id": "25:2/q18/p2", "position": "Each thing's fixed lifespan, provision, endpoint, and unfolding decrees.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says decrees run through Resurrection and beyond; al-Kalbī names form, endpoint and lifespan, Abū Isḥāq livelihood. Al-Qurṭubī includes the hereafter; Yahyā reports ʿAlī illustrating all-encompassing measure with a fingertip-to-tongue gesture. Study Quran connects this to predestination of every phase of creaturely existence."}, {"id": "25:2/q18/p3", "position": "God guided each creature toward what suits it.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this as another account of the divine determining; Mujāhid's animal report says God taught animals what benefits them."}, {"id": "25:2/q18/p4", "position": "God's measure is knowledge of each creature's whole existence, without conjecture.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says divine knowledge and truthful disclosure cannot fail, whereas human estimation can; divine command and will can therefore diverge. Study Quran relays his distinction between human conjecture and God's eternal unchanging knowledge."}, {"id": "25:2/q18/p5", "position": "Each thing's bounds and relations are set within an ordered cosmos.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says determination precedes and accompanies particular existence and relationships, citing 15:21, 54:49, 87:2–3, 57:22 and 64:11; prior and concurrent causes determine effects within God's order. Islahi points to lifespans, clouds, winds, sun and moon, with 36:38 and 15:21; Kuranyolu says no power can violate the appointed laws. Elmalılı stresses bounds and all decreed circumstances."}, {"id": "25:2/q18/p6", "position": "God alone knows the precise successive stages and hidden measures of creation.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥusayn, transmitted by al-Sulamī, gives variant sequences, one from light through soul, spirit, form, names, qualities, time and measures, another from time through power, substance, sound and spirit; the sequences vary, while their hidden precision belongs to God."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q19", "question": "Why say 'created' and then 'measured'?", "turns_on": "How to avoid or interpret the apparent repetition between khalq and taqdīr.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q19/p1", "position": "Creation is bringing into being; the following verb adds its exact measure and fitness.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Samīn reject repeated estimation; al-Bayḍāwī and Abū Ḥayyān report creation as production and subsequent measurement of that production. Al-Ālūsī offers this as one resolution; Ibn ʿĀshūr says measurement excludes chance and shows knowledge and will."}, {"id": "25:2/q19/p2", "position": "Creation is proportioning; the following verb adds preparation for the intended purpose.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives al-Zajjāj's preferred distinction and says a mere inversion of the wording cannot cure repetition without such distinct senses."}, {"id": "25:2/q19/p3", "position": "The measured act of creation is restated to emphasize perfect proportion.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, as reported by Abū Ḥayyān, says wise creation occurs according to measure without disparity; al-Bayḍāwī reports measured production prevents unevenness. {"id": "25:2/q21", "question": "What does the measure imply about divine power, knowledge, and oneness?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q21/p1", "position": "Precise creation manifests omniscience, omnipotence, deliberate will, and sole lordship.", "reasons": "Study Quran links taqdīr to created order and divine knowledge and power. {"id": "25:2/q22", "question": "How do the attributes of verse 2 relate to the revelation in verse 1 and the idols in verse 3?", "turns_on": "The sources trace the sequence either from revelation to refutation of idols, from creation back to ownership, or through accepted premises around contested denials.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q22/p1", "position": "They identify the revealer as sole sovereign and expose the following idols' lack of divinity.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says after divine attributes the passage attacks Quraysh's gods in 25:3, which lack them. Al-Biqāʿī says the sequence elaborates revealer, Furqān and recipient from 25:1; Abū Ḥayyān connects 24:64's ownership with this added kingship. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the repeated relative shifts from gratitude for revelation to oneness. Islahi says the verse moves from beneficence in revelation to power and unity; Kuranyolu reads a response to Meccan claims and all denials of unity."}, {"id": "25:2/q22/p2", "position": "Creation explains sole ownership and the denial of child and partner.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī transmits Irshād al-ʿAql al-Salīm's explanation of the prior denials, al-Ṭībī's prelude of ownership and 6:101 analogy, and an intensification of the next verse's condemnation. Elmalılı calls the waw explanatory and resumptive: universal origination answers how God acquired and governs so vast a realm. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says ownership, universal creation and direct determination answer the pagan proposal of delegated lords; he declines to discuss other interpretations of this and the previous verse as unhelpful."}, {"id": "25:2/q22/p3", "position": "Accepted ownership and creation frame disputed claims of child and partner.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says polytheists conceded God owned heaven and earth and created all things, citing 23:86–87; putting these around the two denials gives the disputed claims a familiar premise and conclusion, while wise action cannot be futile."}, {"id": "25:2/q22/p4", "position": "The verse joins revelation to the same majestic creative order seen in nature.", "reasons": "Asad's introduction cites 25:2 alongside 25:30, 45, 54, 61 and 62, and says the Prophet's complaint about neglect of the Qurʾān remains especially relevant."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q23", "question": "What occasion-like report illustrates God's formation and decree?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q23/p1", "position": "ʿUzayr's prayer recounts human formation, nurture, death, and restoration by God.", "reasons": "Wahb ibn Munabbih transmits the prayer through Ibn Abī Ḥātim: bodies in wombs receive limbs, senses, life, nourishment, scripture, death and resurrection."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q24", "question": "What is reported about the surah's place of revelation and length?", "turns_on": "The minority report reverses the usual classification for the body of the surah.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q24/p1", "position": "Sūrat al-Furqān is Meccan and has seventy-seven verses.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī states the count and classification and transmits Meccan reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn al-Zubayr."}, {"id": "25:2/q24/p2", "position": "Most of the surah is Madinan, with verses 68–70 Meccan.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this minority classification, differing from the Meccan reports."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q25", "question": "What recitation reports concern Sūrat al-Furqān?", "turns_on": "The reports concern different incidents, one variant recitation and the other a mistaken omission.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q25/p1", "position": "The Prophet approved two differing recitations as revealed and taught seven modes.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī reports ʿUmar challenging Hishām ibn Ḥakīm, then the Prophet approving both and directing recitation of what is easy."}, {"id": "25:2/q25/p2", "position": "The Prophet corrected a mistaken claim that an omitted verse had been abrogated.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī transmits Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān's report: after dawn prayer Ubayy ibn Kaʿb thought an omitted verse was abrogated; the Prophet corrected him."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q26", "question": "How is Sūrat al-Furqān's opening situated in its larger theme?", "turns_on": "The notes highlight either the chapter's argumentative mission or its revelation-and-nature theme.", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q26/p1", "position": "The opening defends revelation and prophethood while answering denials of oneness and the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Islahi says the chapter's core is prophethood: it answers Quraysh and allies on Muhammad and the Qurʾān, promises believers reward after trial, and warns persistent deniers. The first nine verses oppose claims of fabrication and conspiracy; opponent propaganda aims to turn people from the Prophet and Qurʾān. Islahi also places the chapter amid a larger sequence about warning, migration, war, monotheism, prophethood and the Hereafter; he says al-Aḥzāb supplements its chapter as al-Nūr does the prior chapter."}, {"id": "25:2/q26/p2", "position": "The chapter's cited natural signs place revelation within divine creative order.", "reasons": "Asad links revelation and nature and notes the Prophet's complaint about abandoned Qurʾān as pertinent today."}]}
{"id": "25:2/q27", "question": "What cross-reference does Asad give for God's sole sovereignty?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "25:2/q27/p1", "position": "He directs the reader to his note on 17:111.", "reasons": "Asad gives note 133 on 17:111 without supplying its content here."}]}
{"id": "25:32/q01", "question": "Who made the objection?", "turns_on": "Whether the speech is attributed to Quraysh/polytheists or to Jews or Christians.", "positions": [{"id": "25:32/q01/p1", "position": "Quraysh or the Arab polytheists.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿĀshūr identify Quraysh or polytheists; al-Ālūsī says the epithet condemns their disbelief, and Abū Ḥayyān calls this the apparent referent."}, {"id": "25:32/q01/p2", "position": "Jews.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and others report that Jews compared the Torah; Ibn ʿĀshūr says this would be slander, and Abū Ḥayyān calls this identification pointless."}, {"id": "25:32/q01/p3", "position": "Jews or Christians.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports this wider alternative and rejects their alleged premise about their scriptures."}, {"id": "25:32/q01/p4", "position": "The disbelievers, without a narrower identification.", "reasons": "The early reports put the demand in unbelievers' mouths; Ibn ʿAbbās relates the polytheists' challenge and Qatāda compares Moses and Jesus."}]}
{"id": "25:32/q02", "question": "What does lawlā mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "25:32/q02/p1", "position": "Why not? or if only, expressing a demand.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā glosses it as why not; Biqāʿī gives why not or if only; Bursevī calls it exhortation."}]}
